intro: A stuffed animal leaking stuffing. A coat with no top button on the coldest day of the year. A seam that split when you bent over. Every one of these is a small problem that a needle and a piece of thread can fix in minutes. You do not need a machine. You need a small kit and a few skills.

In this unit you learn the tools in a sewing kit and the safe way to handle sharp needles and pins. You learn to thread a needle, tie a knot that anchors the thread, and sew two stitches: the running stitch for speed and the back stitch for strength. Then you put those skills to work sewing on a button and mending a split seam.

By the end, you will be able to fix a button so it stays fixed, close a seam from the inside so the fix does not show, and make a small felt project of your own. You will also know why fixing a piece of clothing usually beats throwing it away, for your wallet and for the trash pile.
bigQuestion: How do a needle, a thread and a knot turn a torn thing back into a useful thing?

timeline.t: People carve needles with eyes from bone and sew animal skins together with sinew.
Buttons with buttonholes become a common way to fasten clothing in Europe.
Steel needles are made in Europe, sharper and stronger than bone or bronze.
Charles Weisenthal patents a needle meant for a sewing machine that does not yet exist.
Barthelemy Thimonnier builds an early sewing machine in France.
Elias Howe patents a machine that makes a lockstitch with two threads.
Walter Hunt invents the safety pin, a pin with its point covered.
Isaac Singer sells a sewing machine that works at home and in shops.
Ready-made clothes fill stores, and fewer families sew their own clothing.
Mending comes back as a way to save money and keep cloth out of landfills.

words.d: a thin steel tool with a point on one end and an eye on the other
the hole in a needle that the thread goes through

a small cap worn on the middle finger to push the needle

test.q: Which tool has an eye for the thread?
test.why: A needle has a point and an eye. A pin has a round head instead.

test.q: Where do pins go while you sew?
test.why: The pincushion covers the points; a pin in your mouth could be swallowed.

test.q: Why do you count pins before and after sewing?
choices: So none are lost on the floor
test.why: A lost pin can end up in a rug or a chair.

test.q: How do you pick a thread color for a repair?
choices: Hold spools against the cloth and pick the closest

test.q: The thread will not go through the eye. What helps?
choices: Snip a fresh slanted end and hold close to the tip
test.why: A sharp slanted end held close to the tip goes straight into the eye.

test.q: What does the knot at the end of the thread do?
choices: Stops the thread from pulling through the cloth
test.why: The knot is the anchor for the first stitch.

test.q: Where should knots and loose ends be?
test.why: The wrong side hides knots so the front looks clean.

test.q: Which stitch makes a solid line that will not pull open?
test.why: Each back stitch locks into the one before it.

test.q: The cloth bunched up as you sewed. What went wrong?
test.why: Pulling too hard gathers the cloth. Pull just snug.

test.q: What happens if you cut the thread with no finishing knot?
test.why: Nothing holds the last stitch, so the line comes undone.

test.q: What is the shank under a button for?
choices: To leave room for the buttonhole cloth
test.why: The stem of thread lets the buttonhole cloth slide under without puckering.

test.q: How do you leave room for a shank?
choices: Sew over a toothpick, then pull it out and wrap the thread
test.why: The toothpick leaves slack that you wrap into a firm stem.

test.q: How do you mend a split seam?
choices: Sew on the right side with big stitches
Turn it inside out and back stitch along the old line
test.why: Inside out, with new stitches over the old line, the fix is strong and hidden.

test.q: What do you do when the needle reaches a pin?
test.why: Sewing over a pin can bend the needle or sew the pin into the seam.

test.q: Why does mending usually beat throwing away?
choices: It costs cents and keeps cloth out of the landfill
test.why: A fix costs a little thread and a few minutes; a new piece costs dollars and adds to the trash.

write.prompt: A friend's shirt has lost a button, and the side seam has split. Write the steps to fix both, in order, from opening the sewing kit to putting it away. For each step, name the tool and explain why the step is there.
tips: Put the steps in order, and start with the sewing kit and the safety rules.
Name the tool for each step: needle, thread, pins, scissors, toothpick.
Say which stitch you use for the seam and why it is the strong one.
Explain the knot at the start, the shank under the button, and the knot at the end.
Finish with counting the pins and putting everything back.
